analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $7.15 and extends it to the Northern Mariana Islands.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill: it sat in committee for nearly six months and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have lifted the federal minimum wage from its then-level of $5.15 an hour in three steps: to $6.00, then $6.75, then $7.15, reaching the top rate about a year after passage. It would also have applied the federal minimum wage to the Northern Mariana Islands for the first time, phasing the local wage up 50 cents every six months until it matched the federal rate. It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage, who would see roughly a 39% raise phased in over about a year, plus workers in the Northern Mariana Islands, who would gradually get the same wage floor as the rest of the country.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $6.00 an hour 60 days after enactment, $6.75 six months later, and $7.15 one year after that.

Makes the federal minimum wage apply to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, which had been exempt, starting at $3.55 an hour and rising 50 cents every six months until it reaches the federal rate.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum-wage wages — restaurants, retail stores, and other low-wage businesses — would bear the higher payroll costs, and consumers might see some of that passed on in prices. In the Northern Mariana Islands, employers accustomed to a much lower wage floor would face a phased-in increase.

drawbacks.text: A roughly 39% increase in the minimum wage over about a year raises labor costs for businesses that rely on minimum-wage workers, and opponents argued this could reduce hiring or hours for the least experienced workers.

The Northern Mariana Islands provision would more than double the local wage floor within a few years, a faster change than some island employers — including the garment manufacturing sector — said their economy could absorb, even with the gradual transition schedule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is the standard one for any minimum wage increase: a meaningful pay raise for the lowest-paid workers, paid for by higher labor costs spread across low-wage employers and somewhat higher prices. The phase-in schedule (60 days, 6 months, 12 months) is fairly rapid but not abrupt, and the CNMI transition is gradual enough to soften the shock. The bill was simply written — no tax offsets or carve-outs — which made it easy to understand but also meant its costs fell directly on employers with no cushion.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat with no hearings or votes until the 109th Congress ended and it expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Sherwood Boehlert and 14 House Republican cosponsors introduced the bill on July 13, 2006.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced.
On September 19, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and the record shows no further action of any kind.
The bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers paying the federal minimum wage kept paying the old rate with no increase, and no new wage floor was applied to the Northern Mariana Islands. Workers who would have received the raise gained nothing from this bill's fate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers kept the old wage floor

for.name: Rep. Sherwood Boehlert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the federal minimum wage to $7.15 and extend it to the Northern Mariana Islands.

for.name: 14 of 232 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican, including moderate and Northeast members such as Shays, Leach, Walsh, and King.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the minimum wage
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it was sent to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and remained there until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored entirely by Republicans (14 cosponsors, all R), but the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it, and no Democrats are recorded as sponsors — so no vote ever revealed where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would have raised their wage floor from $5.15 to $7.15 within about a year, increasing payroll costs. The same increase is the wage gain for millions of minimum-wage workers, so the industry's interest ran directly against the workers' interest in this bill.

industries.industry: Garment and other employers in the Northern Mariana Islands
industries.note: The islands had long been exempt from the federal minimum wage, allowing wages far below the U.S. floor. The bill would have ended that exemption on a gradual schedule, raising costs for island manufacturers and other employers while raising pay for local workers.
